legend-hero.purpose: The tab title in the title block. One per view.

plate-header.purpose: The engraved strip across the top of a bay panel.

plate-label.purpose: Field labels, table headers, tags, nav group headings.

reading.purpose: A measured value with its own scale.

data.purpose: Every table cell, timestamp and measured value; tabular figures.

prose.purpose: Explanatory copy, capped at 66ch. Platform stack on purpose.

micro-tag.purpose: Role pills and inline config chips; must not out-weigh the value beside it.

pill-label.purpose: Status pills, title-block cartouche, one-line legend. The most repeated small step.

shadows.name: groove
shadows.purpose: The cross-section of an engraved groove. Every resting surface. This is the material, not decoration.

shadows.name: pressed
shadows.purpose: Active controls, selected chips, the active nav item — a panel switch pushed in.

shadows.name: spine
shadows.purpose: The active bay in the index; the only active cue that survives the collapsed rail.

shadows.name: float
shadows.purpose: Modals and the login card — things that genuinely leave the board.

motion.name: ease-panel
motion.purpose: The single transition token. Colour and border state only, never layout.

motion.name: lamp-test
motion.purpose: The one authored moment: on tab entry the board runs a lamp test, like a real panel at power-up.

motion.name: plate-drop
motion.purpose: Modals and the login plate settling into place.

motion.name: reduced-motion
motion.value: all animation and transition durations collapse to 0.001ms
motion.purpose: Honoured globally; the lamp test is decorative and must not fire.

breakpoints.name: ultrawide
breakpoints.value: 1700px (min-width; reading clamps to 1560px, tables never clamp)

renditions.note: Two authored renditions of one drawing, not a colour inversion. Selection order: stored preference, else prefers-color-scheme. A pre-paint inline script applies the stored value before first paint so the board never flashes the wrong polarity.
renditions.light: Engraved laminate plate. Groove highlight rgba(255,255,255,0.85) over shadow rgba(30,36,32,0.28). Grain 0.13 at baseFrequency 0.8.
renditions.dark: SCADA console in slate, never black. Groove highlight rgba(255,255,255,0.07) over shadow rgba(0,0,0,0.45). Grain 0.09 at baseFrequency 0.65.

components.name: Primary Control
components.description: The single ink block per view. Not a colour — the highest-contrast ink available on the plate, which inverts between renditions.

components.name: Destructive Control
components.description: Outlined until deliberately focused, and kept 18px clear of its neighbours. Panel discipline, where a mis-press costs an outage.
components.css: .ds-ctl { display:inline-flex; align-items:center; justify-content:center; gap:8px; padding:9px 14px; border-radius:2px; border:1px solid var(--border-strong,#8b9188); background:transparent; color:var(--text,#16191c); font-family:'Saira Condensed','Arial Narrow',sans-serif; font-weight:600; font-size:13px; letter-spacing:0.1em; text-transform:uppercase; cursor:pointer; transition:background 140ms, color 140ms, border-color 140ms; } .ds-ctl-secondary:hover { background:var(--surface-3,#cbcec5); } .ds-ctl-danger { color:var(--lamp-fault-ink,#9d2b20); border-color:var(--lamp-fault,#c0392b); margin-left:18px; } .ds-ctl-danger:hover, .ds-ctl-danger:focus-visible { background:var(--lamp-fault,#c0392b); color:#ffffff; } .ds-ctl-danger:focus-visible { outline:2px solid var(--focus,#16191c); outline-offset:2px; }

components.name: Recessed Field

narrative.overview:
Every substation has a wall that is the network: a mimic board, where the bus bars are engraved into laminate, each bay hangs off the bus in the same place it occupies in the yard, and an isolator's state is legible from across the control room because its shape changes, not just its colour. When those boards moved to screens they became the SCADA one-line, and the notation survived the move intact. SentinelNet is drawn as that board. The estate is a one-line diagram indexed by bay; the tables are cable schedules; the panels are engraved plates; and the thing that tells you something is wrong is a lamp, not a chart.

The system exists in two renditions, and neither is the default. The light rendition is the physical board: a cool grey-green laminate plate, black engraved lettering, grooves catching a highlight along their top edge. The dark rendition is its SCADA successor: slate, not black, because a control screen is never off. They are not a colour inversion of each other — the engraving direction flips, the grain coarsens and fades, the lamps shift to screen luminance. Both are real artifacts of the same tradition, and the interface picks up whichever the operating system asks for until someone says otherwise.

The load-bearing rule is that colour means state and nothing else. There is no accent colour in this system. Hierarchy is made of engraving depth, ink weight, letterspacing and space; emphasis is the highest-contrast ink block on the plate. That constraint is what buys the lamps their power: when the only coloured things on a screen are the four indicator states and the conductors of a diagram, a single amber lens is impossible to miss from across a room. It also means the board still works for an operator who cannot distinguish those hues — every state carries a distinct geometry as well.
keyCharacteristics: Two authored renditions of one drawing, never a theme toggle
Colour is state; hierarchy is engraving, weight and space
Square corners everywhere; the only curve in the system is a lamp lens
State is carried by symbol geometry first and colour second
Legend capitals for structure, monospace for every measured value
A plate grain, not a 1px bevel, carries the material

rules.name: The Colour Is State Rule
rules.body: Colour carries state and diagram identity. It is never emphasis, never brand, never decoration. A heading icon tinted amber regardless of what the heading says is the exact violation this rule exists to catch. If something needs to stand out and is not a state, give it ink weight, size, or space.

rules.name: The Geometry First Rule
rules.body: Every state must be distinguishable with all colour removed. A new state needs a new shape before it is allowed a new hue, and the legend must draw that shape by reusing the real component, never a hand-styled copy of it.

rules.name: The Unpolled Is Not Fault Rule
rules.body: Never-interrogated and unreachable are different facts and must never share a symbol. Absence of data is its own state.

rules.name: The Measured Value Rule
rules.body: Anything an engineer compares against another number — counts, ports, VLANs, byte totals, timestamps, meter readings — is set in the data face with tabular figures. Prose numbers stay in prose.

rules.name: The Uppercase Ceiling Rule
rules.body: Uppercase belongs to 13px and below, where wide tracking makes it an engraved legend. Titles are never uppercased; at 17px and up the condensed face is already doing the work.

rules.name: The Tables Don't Clamp Rule
rules.body: Reading widths are capped; data widths are not. A firewall policy has twelve columns and needs every pixel an ultrawide offers.

rules.name: The Isolation Gap Rule
rules.body: A destructive control keeps 18px of empty space between it and its neighbours, and stays outlined until deliberately focused. Borrowed from the panel discipline it is named after, where the consequence of a mis-press is measured in outages.

rules.name: The Engraved Depth Rule
rules.body: Depth comes from a groove and a tone step. If two surfaces do not read as separate, the tone step is wrong — adding a drop shadow is not the fix.

rules.name: The Grain Must Read Rule
rules.body: A material that computes to two levels out of 255 is a token, not a material. Attenuate the grain in exactly one place so its strength stays legible and adjustable.

rules.name: The One Curve Rule
rules.body: If it is round, it is a lamp or it depicts one. Rounding a container is how this system stops looking like itself.

dos: Do carry every state in a distinct geometry first, then colour.
Do make the primary action the ink block — one per view.
Do set every measured value in Azeret Mono with tabular figures.
Do keep both renditions authored: any new token needs a light value and a dark value, and neither may be derived by inverting the other.
Do self-host any new face in static/fonts/ and reference it via @font-face. The exe bundles static/ wholesale, so it ships automatically.
Do resolve tokens through cssVar() before handing a colour to a canvas library (vis.js, xterm.js) — those cannot parse var().
Do give a destructive control its 18px of isolation.
Do say why a section is empty or withheld, rather than removing it.
Do add both an it and an en entry to static/js/i18n.js for every new string.
donts: Don't introduce an accent colour. There isn't one, and adding one dissolves the rule that makes the lamps legible.
Don't round a container. Square is the form language; 2px on controls is the entire allowance.
Don't add a drop shadow to a resting surface — fix the tone step instead.
Don't animate width, height, padding or margin.
Don't use the CVSS ramp for anything that is not a CVSS rating.
Don't let a background: shorthand overwrite a surface — use background-color, or the plate grain is silently erased.
Don't create a stacking context (isolation, z-index on a wrapper, transform on an ancestor) around content that contains dropdowns or modals.
Don't load a font, icon or library from a CDN without a local fallback: isolated management LANs are a confirmed deployment.
Don't hide a first-viewport element behind a role gate without leaving an explanation in its place.
Don't use the on-lamp ink on a wash — a wash sits over a plate, so the -ink lamp variants apply there.
